content: This document on adult immunization serves as a supplement to the General Recommendations on Immunization issued by the Immunization Practices Advisory Committee (ACIP) and updates the previous supplement published in September 1984. It provides a comprehensive overview of adult immunization, including specific vaccine recommendations, information on vaccine-preventable diseases, indications for vaccine use, and details on toxoids and immune globulins recommended for adults. Additionally, it outlines potential side effects, adverse reactions, precautions, and contraindications associated with these immunobiological agents. The document also includes immunization recommendations tailored to specific adult age groups and individuals with unique immunization needs due to factors such as occupation, lifestyle, travel, environmental exposure, or health status. It serves as a compendium of ACIP recommendations but will not be updated regularly. Instead, the ACIP periodically reviews individual immunization statements, which are published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR). Readers are advised to consult these detailed, up-to-date individual statements alongside this compendium to stay informed about current immunization practices. General Considerations Historically, immunization policies have focused primarily on vaccinating infants, children, and adolescents. While vaccination is a routine part of pediatric care, it is less commonly emphasized in the care of adults. The widespread implementation of childhood vaccination programs has significantly reduced the incidence of many vaccine-preventable diseases. However, childhood vaccination alone cannot eliminate certain disease problems. A substantial proportion of the remaining morbidity and mortality from vaccine-preventable diseases occurs among older adolescents and adults. Individuals who have not been naturally infected or vaccinated against diseases such as diphtheria, tetanus, measles, mumps, rubella, and poliomyelitis remain at risk for these diseases and their complications. Several factors have influenced the underutilization of vaccines among adults, including a lack of awareness about the safety and benefits of vaccines, unfounded concerns about adverse reactions, and missed opportunities by healthcare providers to vaccinate adults during office, clinic, or hospital visits. To address this issue and improve adult immunization rates, the National Coalition for Adult Immunization (NCAI) was established in 1988. Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (MMR) Vaccination Adults born after 1956 who lack evidence of immunity to measles, mumps, or rubella should receive the MMR vaccine. Acceptable evidence of immunity includes documentation of vaccination with at least one dose of live MMR vaccine administered on or after the first birthday, laboratory evidence of immunity, or a physician-diagnosed case of measles or mumps. For rubella, physician diagnosis is not considered adequate evidence of immunity. Individuals at higher risk, such as healthcare workers, college students, and international travelers, should have documentation of two doses of live MMR vaccine or other evidence of immunity. During measles outbreaks, all individuals at risk should have evidence of immunity, which includes two doses of live measles vaccine given at least one month apart after the first birthday. Similarly, during mumps or rubella outbreaks, individuals at risk should have evidence of immunity to these diseases. Diphtheria and Tetanus Vaccination All adults should complete a primary series of diphtheria and tetanus toxoids if they have not already done so. A primary series for adults consists of three doses of diphtheria and tetanus toxoid-containing preparations, with the first two doses given at least four weeks apart and the third dose administered 6–12 months after the second. Adults who have completed the primary series should receive a booster dose every 10 years. The Td (tetanus-diphtheria) vaccine is recommended to enhance protection against both diseases. Individuals with unknown or uncertain vaccination histories should be considered unvaccinated and should receive the full three-dose primary series of Td. Influenza and Pneumococcal Vaccination Older adults (≥65 years) and those with high-risk conditions should receive an annual influenza vaccine. Additionally, a single dose of pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is recommended for all adults aged 65 years and older. For individuals with certain high-risk conditions, such as chronic renal failure or immunosuppression, revaccination may be necessary. Hepatitis B Vaccination Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection poses a significant occupational hazard for healthcare and public safety workers who are exposed to blood or blood-contaminated body fluids. Vaccination is recommended for all individuals at risk of occupational exposure to HBV. This includes healthcare workers, public safety workers, and selected staff in institutions for the developmentally disabled. The HB vaccine provides protection for at least seven years, and booster doses are not routinely recommended during this interval. The need for later booster doses will be assessed as more data become available. Rabies Vaccination Veterinarians, animal handlers, and laboratory workers who are at risk of rabies exposure should receive pre-exposure prophylaxis with the human diploid cell rabies vaccine (HDCV). Pre-exposure vaccination simplifies post-exposure therapy by eliminating the need for human rabies immune globulin (HRIG) and reducing the number of post-exposure vaccine doses required. Individuals at continued risk of frequent exposure should receive a booster dose of HDCV every two years or have their serum tested for rabies antibody levels every two years. Travel Vaccinations International travelers are at increased risk of exposure to vaccine-preventable diseases, depending on the regions they visit. Before traveling, individuals should ensure they are up to date on routine vaccinations, including MMR, diphtheria, tetanus, and polio. In many countries, measles, mumps, and rubella remain uncontrolled, and travelers should be immune to these diseases before departure. For travelers to developing countries, additional vaccines, such as hepatitis A, typhoid, and yellow fever, may be recommended based on the specific risks associated with their destination. Special Populations Certain populations, such as inmates of long-term correctional facilities, residents of institutions for the developmentally disabled, and homeless individuals, are at increased risk of vaccine-preventable diseases. These groups should receive appropriate vaccinations, including those for hepatitis B, influenza, and pneumococcal disease. Inmates and residents of such facilities should also be vaccinated against measles, mumps, and rubella, with MMR being the vaccine of choice if susceptibility to multiple diseases is likely. Occupational Considerations Individuals in specific occupations, such as healthcare workers, laboratory personnel, and public safety workers, may require additional vaccines based on their risk of exposure to certain diseases. For example, healthcare workers should receive annual influenza vaccination to reduce the risk of transmitting the virus to high-risk patients. Laboratory workers handling orthopoxviruses or Bacillus anthracis should receive smallpox or anthrax vaccines, respectively.
